tagline: From Richwood’s lumber country to a parkway built for mountain views.
intro: The Highland Scenic Highway climbs from 2,325 feet near Richwood to more than 4,500 feet in the Allegheny Highlands and Plateau. This paved, two-lane National Scenic Byway runs 43 miles through the Monongahela National Forest. FHWA highlights hardwood-covered slopes, high-elevation spruce and a narrow, steep-walled valley, recommending two hours to drive or four to explore. The parkway follows mountain ridges along the Allegheny Front, with overlooks toward Cranberry Glades and Cranberry Wilderness to the west and the Ridge-and-valley Appalachians to the east.

Richwood’s Cherry River Navy, a civic organization, campaigned for the missing Route 39 link between Richwood and Marlinton. Construction replaced a three-hour journey over indirect routes with a 45-minute drive between the towns. The separate WV 150 parkway was dedicated in 1980, designed to meander along mountain ridges as a scenic road. The state byways guide records state designation in August 1992, followed in 1996 by national recognition for the Highland Scenic Highway, WV 150.

From Richwood, the byway follows the North Fork of the Cherry River toward the Cranberry Mountain visitor center at WV 39/55 and WV 150. Cranberry Glades lies near that junction. Turn north onto the parkway for four overlooks of mountains and valleys before reaching US 219 north of Marlinton.

moments.title: Richwood
moments.text: Richwood’s industrial story began with a railroad reaching Cherry Tree Bottoms in 1898. The town incorporated in 1901, taking a name that referred to the surrounding hardwood forests. A sawmill and factories making clothespins, axe handles and paper turned that timber into products. Downtown’s historic district contains mostly two- and three-story masonry commercial buildings from the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, with storefronts below and housing above. The district joined the National Register of Historic Places in 2001. The Cherry River forms here where its north and south forks meet, with neighborhoods climbing the adjoining hillsides.
moments.notice: Notice the downtown masonry buildings, with storefronts at street level and housing above.

moments.title: Cranberry Glades
moments.text: Cranberry Glades supports plants more commonly associated with northern latitudes, including cranberries, sphagnum moss, purple pitcher plants and sundews. These peat bogs lie at about 3,400 feet in the Allegheny Mountains. Five glades were named in 1911, but the smallest, Little Glade, has since grown over and is no longer recognizable. The botanical area became a National Natural Landmark in 1974. Cranberry vines spread over moss hummocks, flowering pink in summer and fruiting in late September. Red spruce, eastern hemlock, yellow birch and red maple make up much of the surrounding bog forest.

moments.title: Big Spruce Overlook
moments.text: Big Spruce Overlook pairs a mountain view with an account of how the Black Mountain forest changed. Its accessible boardwalk explains the area’s logging and fire history. The WV 150 account describes timbering practices that led to a destructive fire, leaving the area barren for decades. The Forest Service places the highway’s highest point at Black Mountain, at 4,550 feet. Big Spruce is one of four parkway overlooks; the others are Williams River, Little Laurel and Red Lick. Each overlook has a different view into the surrounding valleys, accompanied by a sign describing the area.

practical: Big Spruce Overlook: WV 150 is not maintained in winter and is closed when snow covered. The Forest Service strongly discourages travel November–April. Commercial trucks are prohibited. (checked 2026-10-11)
